q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 5,00,000. Its net cash inflows are Rs 2,00,000 at the end of Year 1 (present value factor at 10% = 0.909), Rs 2,00,000 at the end of Year 2 (present value factor at 10% = 0.826) and Rs 1,50,000 at the end of Year 3 (present value factor at 10% = 0.751). The Net Present Value of the project is:
e: NPV = PV of inflows less outlay: (2,00,000 x 0.909) + (2,00,000 x 0.826) + (1,50,000 x 0.751) = Rs 4,59,650; NPV = 4,59,650 - 5,00,000 = (-) Rs 40,350, so the project fails to recover its cost in present value terms.

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 7,50,000 and is expected to yield a net cash inflow of Rs 2,50,000 at the end of each of the next 4 years. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 4 years at 12% is 3.037. The Net Present Value of the project is:
e: PV of the annuity = 2,50,000 x 3.037 = Rs 7,59,250. NPV = 7,59,250 - 7,50,000 = (+) Rs 9,250; a positive NPV means the project earns more than the 12% required return.

q: A machine costing Rs 5,60,000 generates a net cash inflow of Rs 80,000 per year. Its payback period is:
e: With uniform annual inflows, payback = initial cost / annual inflow = 5,60,000 / 80,000 = 7 years, the time taken for cumulative inflows to equal the outlay.

q: A project costing Rs 6,00,000 yields net cash inflows of Rs 1,50,000 in Year 1, Rs 2,00,000 in Year 2, Rs 2,00,000 in Year 3 and Rs 1,50,000 in Year 4. Its payback period is:
e: Cumulative inflows: Year 1 Rs 1,50,000, Year 2 Rs 3,50,000, Year 3 Rs 5,50,000. The balance Rs 50,000 comes from the Year 4 inflow of Rs 1,50,000, taking 50,000/1,50,000 = 1/3 year = 4 months; payback = 3 years 4 months.

q: A project involves an initial outlay of Rs 4,50,000. The discounted (present) values of its cash inflows are Rs 1,50,000 at the end of Year 1, Rs 1,50,000 at the end of Year 2, Rs 1,20,000 at the end of Year 3 and Rs 60,000 at the end of Year 4. The discounted payback period of the project is:
e: Cumulative discounted inflows: Year 1 Rs 1,50,000, Year 2 Rs 3,00,000, Year 3 Rs 4,20,000. The balance Rs 30,000 comes from the Year 4 discounted inflow of Rs 60,000, taking half a year; discounted payback = 3 years 6 months.

q: A project's Net Present Value is (+) Rs 3,000 at a discount rate of 8% and (-) Rs 3,000 at a discount rate of 10%. By interpolation, its internal rate of return is approximately:
e: IRR is the rate at which NPV is zero. Interpolating between +3,000 at 8% and -3,000 at 10%: IRR = 8 + [3,000/(3,000 + 3,000)] x 2 = 8 + 1 = 9%.

q: The present value of the future cash inflows of a project is Rs 6,30,000 and its initial investment is Rs 7,00,000. The Profitability Index of the project is:
e: Profitability Index = PV of future cash inflows / initial investment = 6,30,000 / 7,00,000 = 0.90. Being below 1, it shows the project does not recover its cost in present value terms.

q: An investment of Rs 10,00,000 is expected to yield an average annual profit after depreciation and tax of Rs 1,20,000. The Average Rate of Return on the initial investment is:
e: ARR = average annual profit after depreciation and tax / initial investment x 100 = 1,20,000 / 10,00,000 x 100 = 12%.

q: Depreciation, though it is not a cash outflow, is relevant in a capital budgeting decision because:

options.A: It is added to the initial outlay of the project
options.B: It reduces the taxable profits and thereby affects the after-tax cash flows of the project
options.C: It increases the salvage value of the asset
options.D: It is completely ignored in the Discounted Cash Flow technique

e: Depreciation itself is a non-cash charge, but it is tax-deductible: it reduces taxable profit, saves tax and so increases the after-tax cash flows of the project, which is why it matters in capital budgeting.

q: In capital budgeting, decisions are based on estimated cash flows rather than on accounting profits mainly because:

options.A: Cash flows take into account the actual timing of receipts and payments and exclude non-cash items
options.B: Accounting profits of long-term projects are always higher than their cash flows
options.C: Accounting profits cannot be computed for projects with a life of more than one year
options.D: Income tax is charged on cash flows and not on profits

e: Cash flows record the actual movement of cash, when it is received or paid, and exclude non-cash items like depreciation; decisions rest on them because money has time value and only cash can be reinvested or spent.

q: Two mutually exclusive projects have unequal lives. For a fair comparison between them, the appropriate technique to use is the:

options.C: Simple Net Present Value of the longer project
options.D: Equivalent Annual Annuity (Equivalent Annual Cost) method

e: A simple NPV comparison favours the longer-lived project unfairly. The Equivalent Annual Annuity method converts each project's NPV into an equal annual amount over its life, so projects of unequal lives are compared on a like-for-like yearly basis.

q: Rs 2,00,000 invested today at 10% per annum compound interest will grow in 3 years to (the compound value factor for 3 years at 10% is 1.331):
e: Future value = principal x compound value factor = 2,00,000 x 1.331 = Rs 2,66,200, the amount to which the sum grows with interest compounded annually at 10% for 3 years.

q: A company's capital structure consists of equity capital of Rs 8,00,000 (cost 15%), preference capital of Rs 2,00,000 (cost 11%) and debt of Rs 5,00,000 (after-tax cost 7%). Its weighted average cost of capital is:
A company issues 9% debentures at par. If the tax rate is 50%, the after-tax cost of debt is:
e: Interest on debt is tax-deductible, so after-tax cost = interest rate x (1 - tax rate) = 9% x (1 - 0.50) = 4.5%; the tax saving halves the effective cost.

q: A share is expected to pay a dividend of Rs 4 per share next year. Its market price is Rs 25 and dividends are expected to grow at a constant rate of 4% per year. Using the dividend growth model, the cost of equity is:
e: Cost of equity = D1/P0 + g = 4/25 + 4% = 16% + 4% = 20%, combining the dividend yield on the market price with the constant expected growth rate.

q: Using the Capital Asset Pricing Model, where the risk-free rate is 5%, the expected market return is 11% and the beta of the share is 1.5, the cost of equity is:
e: Under CAPM, cost of equity = risk-free rate + beta x (market return - risk-free rate) = 5% + 1.5 x (11% - 5%) = 5% + 9% = 14%; beta scales the market risk premium.

q: Under the Modigliani-Miller hypothesis (when taxes are ignored), the value of a firm:

options.A: Is independent of its capital structure
options.B: Increases steadily as the proportion of debt increases
options.C: Decreases steadily as the proportion of debt increases
options.D: Is maximum when debt and equity are in equal proportion

e: Under the MM hypothesis without taxes, the total market value of a firm depends only on its operating income and business risk; the way that income is split between debt and equity does not change the firm's value.

q: In EBIT-EPS analysis, the 'indifference point' (break-even level of EBIT) is the level of EBIT at which:

options.A: The enterprise earns no profit and no loss
options.B: The Earnings Per Share is the same under two alternative plans of financing
options.C: The Net Present Value of the project is zero
options.D: The degree of financial leverage is exactly one

e: At the indifference point, two alternative financing plans (for example, debt versus equity) give exactly the same EPS at the same level of EBIT, so management is indifferent between them at that level of earnings.

q: Under the Net Income (NI) approach to capital structure, if the proportion of cheaper debt in the capital structure is increased:

options.A: The weighted average cost of capital rises
options.B: The value of the firm falls
options.C: The weighted average cost of capital remains constant
options.D: The weighted average cost of capital falls and the value of the firm rises

e: The Net Income approach assumes the cost of debt is lower than the cost of equity and both stay constant; adding cheaper debt therefore lowers the overall cost of capital and raises the value of the firm.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 18,00,000, variable costs are Rs 12,00,000 and fixed costs are Rs 3,00,000. The degree of operating leverage is:
e: Degree of operating leverage = contribution / EBIT = (18,00,000 - 12,00,000) / (6,00,000 - 3,00,000) = 6,00,000 / 3,00,000 = 2.0; fixed costs magnify the effect of sales changes on operating profit.

q: An enterprise has earnings before interest and tax of Rs 8,00,000 and pays interest of Rs 3,00,000. Its degree of financial leverage is:
e: Degree of financial leverage = EBIT / (EBIT - interest) = 8,00,000 / (8,00,000 - 3,00,000) = 8,00,000 / 5,00,000 = 1.6.

q: An enterprise has sales of Rs 24,00,000, variable costs of Rs 15,00,000, fixed costs of Rs 5,00,000 and interest of Rs 2,00,000. Its degree of combined leverage is:
e: Degree of combined leverage = contribution / EBT = (24,00,000 - 15,00,000) / (9,00,000 - 5,00,000 - 2,00,000) = 9,00,000 / 2,00,000 = 4.5, combining the operating and financial leverages.

q: The degree of financial leverage of an enterprise is 2. If its earnings before interest and tax increase by 10%, its Earnings Per Share will increase by approximately:
e: Percentage change in EPS = DFL x percentage change in EBIT = 2 x 10% = 20%; financial leverage magnifies the effect of an EBIT change on shareholders' earnings.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 4,00,000 and its current liabilities are Rs 2,50,000. Its current ratio is:
e: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities = 4,00,000 / 2,50,000 = 1.6 : 1, the standard measure of short-term solvency.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 12,00,000, including stock of Rs 5,00,000 and prepaid expenses of Rs 1,00,000. Current liabilities are Rs 5,00,000. The quick (acid-test) ratio is:
e: Quick assets exclude stock and prepaid expenses: 12,00,000 - 5,00,000 - 1,00,000 = Rs 6,00,000. Quick ratio = 6,00,000 / 5,00,000 = 1.2 : 1.

q: Long-term debt of an enterprise is Rs 3,00,000 and its shareholders' funds are Rs 7,50,000. The debt-equity ratio is:
e: Debt-equity ratio = long-term debt / shareholders' funds = 3,00,000 / 7,50,000 = 0.4 : 1, showing the proportion of outside long-term funds to owners' funds.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 25,00,000 and the cost of goods sold is Rs 15,00,000. Its gross profit ratio is:
The net profit of an enterprise is Rs 2,40,000 on sales of Rs 20,00,000. Its net profit ratio is:
e: Net profit ratio = net profit / sales x 100 = 2,40,000 / 20,00,000 x 100 = 12%, the margin earned on sales after all expenses and tax.

q: The cost of goods sold of an enterprise is Rs 20,00,000 and its average inventory is Rs 2,50,000. The inventory turnover ratio is:
e: Inventory turnover = cost of goods sold / average inventory = 20,00,000 / 2,50,000 = 8 times, showing how many times stock is sold and replaced during the year.

q: Credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 18,00,000 and its average debtors are Rs 2,00,000. The debtors turnover ratio is:
e: Debtors turnover = credit sales / average debtors = 18,00,000 / 2,00,000 = 9 times; a higher ratio indicates faster collection from customers.

q: Credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 10,95,000 and its average debtors are Rs 90,000. Taking a year of 365 days, the average collection period is:
e: Average collection period = average debtors / credit sales x 365 = 90,000 / 10,95,000 x 365 = 30 days, the average time taken to collect from debtors.

q: Credit purchases of an enterprise are Rs 7,30,000 and its average creditors are Rs 80,000. Taking a year of 365 days, the average payment period is:
e: Average payment period = average creditors / credit purchases x 365 = 80,000 / 7,30,000 x 365 = 40 days, the average time taken to pay suppliers.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 9,00,000 and the interest payable is Rs 2,00,000. The interest coverage ratio is:
e: Interest coverage = PBIT / interest = 9,00,000 / 2,00,000 = 4.5 times, showing how many times the operating profit covers the interest obligation.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 6,40,000 and its capital employed is Rs 16,00,000. The Return on Capital Employed is:
e: ROCE = PBIT / capital employed x 100 = 6,40,000 / 16,00,000 x 100 = 40%, the return earned on the long-term funds invested in the enterprise.

q: The net profit after tax of a company is Rs 9,00,000 and the preference dividend payable is Rs 1,00,000. If the company has 2,50,000 equity shares, its Earnings Per Share (EPS) is:
e: EPS = (net profit after tax - preference dividend) / number of equity shares = (9,00,000 - 1,00,000) / 2,50,000 = Rs 3.20 per share, the earnings belonging to each equity shareholder.

q: The net profit of an enterprise is Rs 4,00,000, after charging depreciation of Rs 80,000 and goodwill written off of Rs 20,000, and after crediting a profit of Rs 30,000 on the sale of machinery. The funds from operations are:
e: Funds from operations = 4,00,000 + depreciation 80,000 + goodwill written off 20,000 - profit on sale of machinery 30,000 = Rs 4,70,000; non-cash charges are added back and the non-operating profit is removed.

q: An enterprise's operating profit before working capital changes is Rs 5,00,000. During the year, its stock decreased by Rs 45,000 and its creditors decreased by Rs 35,000. The cash from operations is:
e: Cash from operations = 5,00,000 + decrease in stock 45,000 (cash released) - decrease in creditors 35,000 (cash paid out) = Rs 5,10,000.

q: In a cash flow statement prepared under Accounting Standard 3 (AS-3), the cash proceeds from the issue of equity shares are classified as:

options.C: Not shown in the cash flow statement

e: Under AS-3, issuing shares brings in funds from the owners, which is a financing transaction; such proceeds are therefore shown under financing activities, not operating or investing activities.

q: A payment of Rs 50,000 in cash made to trade creditors will, in a fund flow statement, result in:

options.B: No flow of funds, since both the accounts involved are current accounts

e: Payment to trade creditors reduces both cash, a current asset, and creditors, a current liability, by the same amount; working capital is unchanged, so there is no flow of funds in the fund flow sense.

q: During a year, the current assets of an enterprise increased by Rs 1,20,000 and its current liabilities increased by Rs 70,000. The net change in its working capital is:
e: Change in working capital = increase in current assets - increase in current liabilities = 1,20,000 - 70,000 = an increase of Rs 50,000, since working capital is the excess of current assets over current liabilities.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Financial Internal Rate of Return (FIRR) of a railway project measures the return to the Railways themselves, reckoning only their monetary receipts and outgoings.
2. For a new line serving a backward area, the Economic Internal Rate of Return (EIRR) is normally lower than the FIRR, because the wider social benefits are excluded from it.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
e: Statement 1 is correct: FIRR reckons only the Railways' own monetary receipts and outgoings. Statement 2 is wrong: EIRR additionally counts the wider economic and social benefits, so for a backward-area line it is normally higher, not lower, than FIRR. Hence 1 only.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Indian Railways are exempt from paying dividend to General Revenues on the capital-at-charge attributable to strategic lines.
2. The losses on the working of strategic lines are borne by General Finances.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
e: Both statements are correct: no dividend is payable to General Revenues on the capital-at-charge attributable to strategic lines, and the losses on working such lines are borne by General Finances.

q: The net earnings of a railway are Rs 6,000 crore and its capital-at-charge is Rs 1,20,000 crore. The return on capital-at-charge is:
e: Return on capital-at-charge = net earnings / capital-at-charge x 100 = 6,000 / 1,20,000 x 100 = 5%, the measure of Railways' financial performance against the dividend payable to General Revenues.

q: A railway earned gross traffic receipts of Rs 2,80,000 crore against ordinary working expenses of Rs 2,52,000 crore. Its Operating Ratio is:
e: Operating Ratio = ordinary working expenses / gross traffic receipts x 100 = 2,52,000 / 2,80,000 x 100 = 90%; it shows the share of earnings consumed by working expenses, the lower the better.

q: 'Capital-at-charge' of Indian Railways denotes:

options.A: The total capital invested in the Railways out of General Revenues, on which dividend is payable to General Revenues
options.B: The current market value of all railway assets
options.C: The capital raised by the Railways through market borrowings only
options.D: The book value of stores held in stock in the depots

e:
Capital-at-charge is the capital invested in the Railways out of General Revenues, on which dividend is payable to General Revenues; it is not the market value of assets, market borrowings or the value of stores.
Update: capital-at-charge (about Rs 2.27 lakh crore) was wiped off when the Railway Budget merged with the General Budget, and no dividend liability arises from 2017-18; the keyed text states the term's original meaning. (Source: Union Cabinet approval dated 21.09.2016 for the Budget merger, PIB; effective Budget 2017-18.)

q: A 'budget centre' means:

options.A: The office in which the master budget is kept
options.B: A section or part of an organisation for which a separate budget is prepared and whose manager is held responsible for its performance
options.C: The committee which approves the budgets of the enterprise
options.D: The period for which a budget is prepared

e: A budget centre is a distinct section or part of the organisation for which a separate budget is prepared and controlled, with its manager held responsible for the performance of that unit.

q: Budgeted sales of a product are 60,000 units. The opening stock is 7,000 units and the closing stock is to be 10,000 units. The production budget should provide for production of:
e: Production = budgeted sales + closing stock - opening stock = 60,000 + 10,000 - 7,000 = 63,000 units, providing also for the planned build-up of stock.

q: Production of 25,000 units is budgeted, each unit requiring 4 kg of material priced at Rs 10 per kg. The opening stock of material is 6,000 kg and the closing stock is to be 9,000 kg. The value of materials to be purchased is:
e: Material consumed = 25,000 units x 4 kg = 1,00,000 kg. Purchases = consumption + closing stock - opening stock = 1,00,000 + 9,000 - 6,000 = 1,03,000 kg, worth 1,03,000 x Rs 10 = Rs 10,30,000.

q: A cash budget shows an opening cash balance of Rs 60,000, estimated receipts of Rs 4,20,000 and estimated payments of Rs 4,50,000 for a month. The closing cash balance will be:
e: Closing balance = opening balance + receipts - payments = 60,000 + 4,20,000 - 4,50,000 = Rs 30,000; total resources still exceed payments, so no overdraft arises.

q: A budget provides for fixed costs of Rs 3,60,000 and variable costs of Rs 15 per unit. The total flexed budget allowance at an actual output of 20,000 units is:
e: A flexed budget restates variable costs at the actual activity level: 3,60,000 fixed + (20,000 units x Rs 15) = 3,60,000 + 3,00,000 = Rs 6,60,000; the fixed cost element is not flexed.

q: A semi-variable cost amounts to Rs 44,000 at an output of 6,000 units and Rs 56,000 at an output of 10,000 units. The fixed element of the cost is:
e: By the high-low method, variable cost per unit = (56,000 - 44,000) / (10,000 - 6,000) = Rs 3. Fixed element = 44,000 - (6,000 x 3) = 44,000 - 18,000 = Rs 26,000.

q: A drawback of 'imposed' (authoritarian) budgeting, under which targets are set by the top management without the participation of the managers who have to achieve them, is that:

options.A: The managers concerned may lack commitment to the targets and resent them, so that the motivational value of the budget is largely lost
options.B: It takes much more time than participative budgeting
options.C: It cannot be used in a large organisation at all
options.D: It requires every item of expenditure to be justified from a zero base

e: Because the managers who must achieve the targets had no say in setting them, imposed budgets often lack ownership and commitment; the targets may be resented and the budget loses its motivational value.

q: Under zero-base budgeting, the decision packages prepared by the responsibility managers are:

options.A: Approved automatically in the order in which they are received
options.B: Ranked in order of priority or benefit, so that the limited funds available are allocated first to the highest-ranked packages
options.C: Funded equally, irrespective of their relative merit
options.D: Examined only by the statutory auditor of the enterprise

e: Under zero-base budgeting, each activity is justified afresh through decision packages, which are ranked in order of priority or benefit so that the limited funds available are allotted first to the highest-ranked packages.

q: In a manufacturing concern, raw materials are held for 45 days, the production process takes 10 days, finished goods are held for 30 days and debtors take 50 days to pay. Suppliers allow 40 days' credit. The length of the operating cycle is:
e: Gross cycle = raw materials 45 + production 10 + finished goods 30 + debtors 50 = 135 days, less the 40 days' credit taken from suppliers, giving a net operating cycle of 95 days.

q: The annual operating cost of an enterprise is Rs 42,00,000 (reckoning a year of 360 days). Its operating cycle is 60 days. On the operating-cycle method, the working capital required is:
e: Working capital = annual operating cost x operating cycle / 360 = 42,00,000 x 60/360 = Rs 7,00,000, the funds locked up for one cycle of operations.

q: 'Temporary' (fluctuating) working capital refers to:

options.A: The minimum level of current assets which is maintained throughout the year
options.B: The additional working capital required over and above the permanent level to meet seasonal demands or special contingencies, which varies during the year
options.C: Working capital borrowed for a period of less than one month
options.D: The cash balance kept in the office chest

e: Temporary working capital is the additional amount required over and above the permanent level to meet seasonal demands or special contingencies; unlike the permanent minimum, it rises and falls during the year.

q: The current ratio of an enterprise is 2.5 : 1 and its current liabilities are Rs 4,00,000. Its net working capital is:
e: Current assets = 2.5 x current liabilities = 2.5 x 4,00,000 = Rs 10,00,000. Net working capital = 10,00,000 - 4,00,000 = Rs 6,00,000.

q: Under the Tandon Committee's Method II of lending, the maximum permissible bank finance (MPBF) for a borrower with total current assets of Rs 20,00,000 and current liabilities (other than bank borrowings) of Rs 5,00,000 is:
e: Under Tandon Method II the borrower finances 25% of total current assets from long-term sources: MPBF = 75% of current assets - other current liabilities = 15,00,000 - 5,00,000 = Rs 10,00,000.

q: Which of the following is NOT a cost of maintaining receivables?

options.C: Interest (opportunity cost) on the funds blocked in receivables
options.D: Wages paid to the production workers of the factory

e: Costs of maintaining receivables are bad debt losses, collection and credit-administration costs, and interest on the funds blocked in receivables. Wages of production workers are a manufacturing cost, unrelated to receivables.

q: Credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 16,20,000 and its average debtors are Rs 1,35,000. The debtors turnover ratio is:
e: Debtors turnover = credit sales / average debtors = 16,20,000 / 1,35,000 = 12 times.

q: Annual credit purchases of an enterprise are Rs 13,50,000 and its average creditors are Rs 1,50,000. The creditors turnover ratio is:
e: Creditors turnover = credit purchases / average creditors = 13,50,000 / 1,50,000 = 9 times.

q: A supplier offers credit terms of 2/15, net 45. The approximate annual cost of not taking the cash discount (on a 360-day year basis) is:
e: Cost of not taking the discount = [2/(100 - 2)] x [360/(45 - 15)] = 2/98 x 12 = 24.5% per annum; the 2% discount is effectively interest earned for paying 30 days before the due date.

q: In receivables management, credit should be extended to a customer, or the credit period lengthened, so long as:

options.A: Sales keep increasing, whatever the cost involved
options.B: The incremental profit from the additional sales exceeds the incremental cost of the additional investment in receivables, including expected bad debts
options.C: The customer presses for more credit
options.D: Competing firms are granting longer credit

e: Credit should be extended only so long as the incremental profit from the additional sales exceeds the incremental cost of the additional investment in receivables, including interest and expected bad debts; rising sales alone do not justify it.

q: The maximum consumption of a material is 450 units per week and the maximum re-order period is 6 weeks. The re-order level for the material is:
e: Re-order level = maximum consumption x maximum re-order period = 450 x 6 = 2,700 units, fixed so that stock lasts even at the highest usage combined with the longest lead time.

q: The re-order level of a material is 3,200 units. Normal consumption is 250 units per week and the normal re-order period is 8 weeks. The minimum stock level is:
e: Minimum level = re-order level - (normal consumption x normal re-order period) = 3,200 - (250 x 8) = 3,200 - 2,000 = 1,200 units, the safety level below which stock should not normally fall.

q: The re-order level of a material is 4,500 units and the re-order quantity is 3,000 units. Minimum consumption is 150 units per week and the minimum re-order period is 6 weeks. The maximum stock level is:
e: Maximum level = re-order level + re-order quantity - (minimum consumption x minimum re-order period) = 4,500 + 3,000 - (150 x 6) = 7,500 - 900 = 6,600 units.

q: The main purpose of fixing stock levels (maximum, minimum and re-order levels) for materials is to:

options.A: Maximise the quantity of material kept in the stores
options.B: Fix the personal responsibility of the storekeeper for all shortages
options.C: Avoid the need for maintaining any stores records
options.D: Ensure that materials are available when required, while keeping the investment in stocks and the carrying costs at the minimum

e: Stock levels trigger timely re-ordering and set safe limits, so that materials are available when required while the investment in stocks, and with it carrying costs like interest and storage, is kept at the minimum.

q: The annual consumption of a material is 9,800 units. The cost of placing an order is Rs 50 and the carrying cost is Rs 2 per unit per year. Using EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C), the Economic Order Quantity is:
e: EOQ = sqrt(2 x 9,800 x 50 / 2) = sqrt(4,90,000) = 700 units, the order size at which ordering cost and carrying cost together are at their minimum.

q: In FSN analysis, stores items are classified as Fast-moving, Slow-moving and Non-moving on the basis of:

options.B: Their consumption or movement pattern, that is, how frequently and how recently they have been issued
options.C: Their criticality for production or services

e: FSN analysis classifies items as Fast, Slow and Non-moving according to their consumption or movement pattern - how frequently and how recently they have been issued - not by price, value or criticality.

q: 'Stock-out costs' in inventory management refer to:

options.A: The cost of storing and insuring the stock in the warehouse
options.B: The costs and losses suffered when an item is out of stock, such as production stoppage, loss of sales and goodwill, and emergency purchases at higher prices
options.C: The cash discount lost by not buying in bulk
options.D: The wages of the stores staff

e: Stock-out costs are the costs and losses suffered when an item is out of stock: production stoppage, loss of sales and goodwill, and emergency purchases at higher prices; they differ from the costs of holding stock.

q: Under the Baumol model of cash management, an enterprise's annual cash requirement is Rs 24,50,000, the cost of converting marketable securities into cash is Rs 20 per transaction and the opportunity interest rate is 8% per annum. The optimum cash balance, sqrt(2AT/i), is:
e: Optimum cash balance = sqrt(2 x 24,50,000 x 20 / 0.08) = Rs 35,000. The Baumol model balances the fixed cost of converting securities into cash against the interest forgone on the cash balance held.

q: Under the Miller-Orr model of cash management, an enterprise fixes a lower control limit of Rs 12,000 and a return point of Rs 30,000. The upper control limit is:
e: In the Miller-Orr model, upper limit = 3 x return point - 2 x lower limit = (3 x 30,000) - (2 x 12,000) = 90,000 - 24,000 = Rs 66,000; the spread above the return point is twice that below it.

q: The basic objective of cash management is to:

options.A: Keep the maximum possible amount of cash idle in the bank
options.B: Avoid all bank borrowings in every circumstance
options.D: Maintain just enough liquidity to meet the obligations of the enterprise, while ensuring that surplus cash does not remain idle and unproductive

e: The basic objective of cash management is to maintain just enough liquidity to meet the obligations of the enterprise as they fall due, while ensuring that surplus cash does not remain idle and unproductive.

q: 'Synchronisation of cash flows', as a technique of cash management, means:

options.A: Keeping the cash of the enterprise in several banks at the same time
options.B: Arranging the pattern of cash receipts and payments so that they coincide as closely as possible, thereby reducing the need for idle balances and short-term borrowing
options.C: Preparing the cash budget at the same time as the sales budget
options.D: Making all payments on a single fixed day of the month

e: Synchronisation of cash flows means arranging the pattern of receipts and payments so that they coincide as closely as possible; cash then turns over quickly, reducing idle balances and the need for short-term borrowing.

q: A division earns a profit of Rs 5,60,000 on capital employed of Rs 32,00,000. The Return on Investment of the division is:
e: ROI = profit / capital employed x 100 = 5,60,000 / 32,00,000 x 100 = 17.5%, the rate of return earned on the funds invested in the division.

q: A division earns a profit of Rs 12,00,000 on capital employed of Rs 80,00,000. The cost of capital is 11%. The Residual Income of the division is:
e: Residual Income = profit - (cost of capital x capital employed) = 12,00,000 - (11% x 80,00,000) = 12,00,000 - 8,80,000 = Rs 3,20,000, the surplus earned after charging for the capital used.

q: The Net Operating Profit After Tax (NOPAT) of a division is Rs 12,50,000, its capital employed is Rs 75,00,000 and the cost of capital is 10%. Its Economic Value Added (EVA) is:
e: EVA = NOPAT - (cost of capital x capital employed) = 12,50,000 - (10% x 75,00,000) = 12,50,000 - 7,50,000 = Rs 5,00,000, the value created after meeting the full cost of the capital employed.

q: Under the negotiated transfer-pricing method:

options.A: The head office fixes the transfer price unilaterally for all divisions
options.B: The transfer price is always the external market price of the product
options.C: No price at all is recorded for goods transferred between divisions
options.D: The buying and selling divisions mutually agree upon the transfer price through bargaining, which preserves divisional autonomy, though the outcome may reflect the bargaining skill of the managers

e: Under the negotiated method, the buying and selling divisions mutually agree the transfer price through bargaining; this preserves divisional autonomy, though the outcome may reflect the relative bargaining skill of the managers rather than pure economics.

q: A division which has spare capacity produces a component at a variable cost of Rs 40 per unit. It has no alternative use for the spare capacity. The minimum transfer price it should accept for transferring the component to another division is:
e: With spare capacity and no alternative use for it, the selling division sacrifices nothing by transferring; the minimum transfer price it should accept is therefore just the variable cost of Rs 40 per unit.

q: The Balanced Scorecard is best described as a framework which:

options.A: Translates an organisation's vision and strategy into a coherent set of objectives and performance measures, covering financial as well as non-financial perspectives
options.B: Is used only for preparing the annual budget of an enterprise
options.C: Replaces the profit and loss account of the enterprise
options.D: Measures only the financial performance of the divisions

e: The Balanced Scorecard translates an organisation's vision and strategy into a coherent set of objectives and performance measures covering financial as well as non-financial perspectives, such as customers, internal processes and learning and growth.

q: In throughput accounting, the sales of a factory for a period are Rs 8,00,000, the direct material cost is Rs 3,00,000 and all other costs, treated as operating expenses, are Rs 3,50,000. The net profit for the period is:
e: Throughput = sales - direct material cost = 8,00,000 - 3,00,000 = Rs 5,00,000. Net profit = throughput - operating expenses = 5,00,000 - 3,50,000 = Rs 1,50,000, all other costs being treated as operating expenses of the period.

q: Management audit differs from internal audit mainly in that:

options.A: It is conducted by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India
options.B: It is concerned only with the checking of cash transactions
options.C: Its scope is much wider, covering an appraisal of the whole management process — objectives, policies, organisation and methods — whereas internal audit is mainly concerned with accounting records and financial controls
options.D: It is compulsory for all companies under the Companies Act

e: Management audit has a much wider scope, appraising the whole management process - objectives, policies, organisation and methods - whereas internal audit is mainly concerned with accounting records, transactions and financial controls.

q: The expected market price of a product is Rs 2,000 per unit and the firm desires a profit margin of 15% on the selling price. The target cost of the product is:
e: Target cost = expected market price - desired profit = 2,000 - (15% x 2,000) = 2,000 - 300 = Rs 1,700; the product must be designed and produced within this cost to earn the required margin.

q: Value analysis, as distinct from value engineering, is applied to:

options.A: Existing products already in production, with a view to eliminating unnecessary costs in them
options.B: Products which are still at the design stage
options.C: Services only, and not to products

e: Value engineering is applied at the design stage of new products; value analysis applies the same scrutiny to existing products already in production, with a view to eliminating unnecessary costs in them.

q: In product life-cycle costing, it is generally recognised that:

options.A: Design-stage decisions have no effect on the costs incurred later
options.B: All the costs of a product are committed only when its production starts
options.C: A major part of a product's life-cycle costs is committed (locked in) at the design and development stage, even though those costs are actually incurred in the later stages
options.D: Life-cycle costs can be reduced most easily at the disposal stage

e: In life-cycle costing, a major part of a product's total costs is committed (locked in) by design and development decisions, even though the costs are actually incurred in the later production, use and disposal stages.

q: In a period of rising prices, under Current Purchasing Power (CPP) accounting, an enterprise which holds net monetary liabilities (monetary liabilities exceeding its monetary assets) experiences:

options.C: A purchasing power gain, because the liabilities will be settled in money of a lower real value
options.D: A gain only in respect of its fixed assets

e: Under CPP accounting in a period of rising prices, monetary liabilities are settled in money of lower real value, so an enterprise holding net monetary liabilities experiences a purchasing power gain; holders of net monetary assets lose.

q: An asset was purchased for Rs 2,50,000 when the general price index stood at 100. At the balance sheet date the index stands at 160. Under the Current Purchasing Power (CPP) method, the restated value of the asset is:
e: Under the CPP method, the asset is restated by the change in the general price index: 2,50,000 x 160/100 = Rs 4,00,000, expressing its cost in units of current purchasing power.

q: Under Flamholtz's stochastic rewards valuation model of human resource accounting, the value of an individual to the organisation is based on:

options.A: The training cost incurred on the individual
options.B: The cost that would be incurred in replacing the individual
options.C: The total earnings of the individual in the past
options.D: The present value of the future services he is expected to render in the various roles (service states) he may occupy, weighted by the probability of his occupying each of them

e: Under Flamholtz's stochastic rewards model, an individual's value is the present value of the future services he is expected to render in the various roles (service states) he may occupy, weighted by the probability of his occupying each of them.

q: The gross working capital of an enterprise is Rs 14,00,000 and its net working capital is Rs 9,00,000. Its current liabilities are:
e: Current liabilities = gross working capital - net working capital = 14,00,000 - 9,00,000 = Rs 5,00,000, since gross working capital is total current assets and net working capital is current assets less current liabilities.

q: In throughput accounting, inventories of work-in-progress and finished goods are valued at:

options.B: Full absorption cost, including fixed overheads
options.D: Totally variable cost only, essentially the direct material cost, all other costs being treated as operating expenses of the period

e: In throughput accounting, inventories are valued at totally variable cost only, essentially the direct material cost, because all other costs are treated as operating expenses of the period and are not attached to stock.

q: 'Discretionary fixed costs' are costs which:

options.A: Cannot be changed in the short run because they arise from past capital decisions, such as depreciation
options.B: Arise from periodic management decisions, such as expenditure on advertising and research, and can be discontinued without immediately affecting operations
options.C: Vary directly with the level of output produced
options.D: Are fixed in total only within a very narrow range of activity

e: Discretionary fixed costs arise from periodic management decisions, such as advertising and research expenditure, and can be discontinued without immediately affecting operations; committed costs like depreciation, arising from past capital decisions, cannot be altered so easily.

q: The 'relevant range' in cost behaviour analysis means:

options.A: The range of activity over which the assumptions about fixed and variable cost behaviour are expected to hold good
options.B: The range of output between the break-even point and full capacity
options.C: The range of prices within which a product can be sold profitably
options.D: The range of activity over which total fixed costs keep on increasing in steps

e: The relevant range is the range of activity over which the assumptions about cost behaviour - fixed costs constant in total and variable cost constant per unit - are expected to hold good.

q: An 'engineered cost' is a cost which:

options.A: Is estimated by the engineers of the factory without any relation to output
options.B: Is incurred only on the construction of plant and machinery
options.C: Has no identifiable relationship with the volume of output
options.D: Has a clear, definite and measurable physical relationship with the input used and the output obtained, such as the cost of direct material

e: An engineered cost has a clear, definite and measurable physical relationship between the input used and the output obtained, such as the cost of direct material, and can be estimated reliably from specifications.

q: Royalty payable on the basis of the number of units produced is treated in cost accounts as:

options.C: A direct expense, forming part of the prime cost of production

e: Royalty payable on the basis of units produced varies with production and is traceable to the product, so it is treated as a direct expense forming part of the prime cost of production.

q: The cost of primary packing of a product — that is, the packing without which the product cannot be sold or handled — is treated as:
e: Primary packing, without which the product cannot be sold or handled, is treated as a production (manufacturing) cost; only secondary packing used for transport or promotion is a selling and distribution cost.

q: Which of the following methods of segregating a semi-variable cost into its fixed and variable elements is generally regarded as the most accurate, as it uses all the observations of the data?
e: The least squares method uses all the observations of the data to fit the cost line statistically, so it is generally the most accurate method of segregating a semi-variable cost; the high-low method uses only two extreme points.

q: The opening stock of a material is 200 units valued at Rs 10 per unit. A further 300 units are purchased at Rs 12 per unit. Under the weighted average price method, the price at which issues will be charged is:
e: Weighted average price = total value / total quantity = (200 x Rs 10 + 300 x Rs 12) / 500 = 5,600 / 500 = Rs 11.20 per unit, the rate at which issues are charged under this method.

q: During a period of continuously rising prices of materials, the FIFO method of pricing issues, as compared with the LIFO method, results in:

options.A: A lower value of closing stock and a lower reported profit
options.B: A higher value of closing stock and a lower reported profit
options.C: The same value of closing stock under both methods
options.D: A higher value of closing stock and a higher reported profit

e: Under FIFO in a period of rising prices, issues are charged at the older, lower prices and closing stock is valued at the latest, higher prices; FIFO therefore gives a higher closing stock and a higher reported profit than LIFO.

q: The cost of material consumed in a factory during a year is Rs 3,60,000 and the average stock of material held is Rs 60,000. The material turnover ratio is:
e: Material turnover ratio = cost of material consumed / average stock of material = 3,60,000 / 60,000 = 6 times, indicating how quickly material stock is consumed and replaced.

q: In cost accounts, a 'material abstract' (material analysis sheet) is a statement which:

options.A: Lists the materials lying in the stores at the end of the year
options.B: Summarises and analyses the material issues made during a period to the various jobs, processes and departments, so as to facilitate their costing
options.C: Records the materials purchased during a period, supplier-wise
options.D: Shows the materials returned by departments to the stores as surplus

e: A material abstract (material analysis sheet) summarises and analyses the material issues made during a period to the various jobs, processes and departments, so that material cost can be charged correctly to each cost unit.
